headline: Survives with a real hole: an EPS beat of 180% smells of one-time revenue, and we cannot see the release
reasoning: priced_in_score: 0.5. The after-hours mark is already +15%, about half to two-thirds of a full re-rate on ANALYST's EBITDA math, and those 160 odd-lot shares say little about the open.

Weakest link, quoted: 'revenue is compounding on volume'. EPS of $0.70 against $0.25 is a 180% beat on a 16% revenue beat. That ratio fits a one-time catch-up, such as Medicare billing or collections on earlier tests (CareDx has had them before), better than run-rate growth. If even $10M of the quarter is one-time, the 'raise bigger than the beat' argument shrinks to a raise about equal to the beat. Neither the summary nor the Benzinga lines break it out.

Against my own objection: the full-year adjusted EBITDA guide went up 32% and the revenue guide went up $30M. Management raised Q4 too, and companies rarely guide a catch-up into the next quarter. The +51% testing volume is not a billing artifact. That is why I do not kill it.

Track record: my 6 kills averaged +1.1% afterwards (3 of 6 right), so I raise my bar. The crew's comparable longs: SMCI (stopped), EXLS (QUANT rejected; it opened -2.2%). Both were modest raises. This raise is larger and Q4-inclusive, which is the distinction ANALYST draws, and it is a fair one.
Who acted first: every screen read 'Beats $0.25 Estimate' at 16:02 ET. The edge, if any, is in the revisions over days, not the first print.
objections: 1. After-hours price on odd lots only (SCOUT).
2. Possible one-time catch-up inside the EPS beat; not broken out (ANALYST, SKEPTIC).
3. +15% after hours already prices a large part of the re-rate.
4. The stock's max daily move in 60 sessions is 13%: a volatile name where stops get hit.
5. The crew's two comparable longs did not work.
